title: Building Cursor Composer – Lee Robinson, Cursor
talk_summary: Cursor describes training their own Composer agent model with RL in an environment that mirrors production, emphasizing parallel tool calls, semantic search, and infrastructure to keep rollouts efficient.

takeaways.technique: Parallel tool calls in the agent harness
takeaways.what_they_do: The agent autonomously decides to run tool calls serially or in parallel, e.g. reading many files at once instead of one by one, which they explicitly trained for and cite as a major speed win.
takeaways.evidence_quote: instead of reading a file one by one, you can read 10 files in parallel with tool calling
takeaways.numbers: ~4x more token-generation efficient than similar-intelligence models (model-level, not harness)

takeaways.technique: Semantic codebase search as a first-class tool
takeaways.what_they_do: They index the codebase with their own embedding model so the agent can make natural-language queries to find files to edit, and found it helped every model in their harness.
takeaways.evidence_quote: semantic search not only helped basically every single model inside of the cursor agent harness

takeaways.what_they_do: Early models made too many unnecessary edits; with more training the model learned to search and read files first, then edit, which they call being 'more effective'.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the model actually got surprisingly better at learning to search and read files more

takeaways.technique: Reuse production-like VM sandboxes for heavy work
takeaways.what_they_do: They spin up cloud VMs per task that load the user's code and let the agent edit/run tools in a secure sandbox, and reuse the same fleet for training because it matches production.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we spin up virtual machines in the cloud ... the perfect Impra for RL and our use in training
takeaways.numbers: hundreds of thousands of VMs in the fleet

takeaways.technique: Load-balance uneven rollouts to avoid idle time
takeaways.what_they_do: Because rollouts finish at different times, they shift work across threads/processes so fast-finishing tasks don't leave workers idle waiting on slow ones.
takeaways.evidence_quote: do load balancing across the different threads and processes to basically shift the work around and and not have a bunch of idle time
